_note: Second-language captions. The two films use different examples (幺/拐 against Bravo/niner), so the Chinese film's English captions translate the Chinese script and the English film's Chinese captions translate the English script; neither film reuses the other's lines. build_timeline.py writes them as each film's second SRT.

zh-film-en.ns00-01: Here's a question: what three digits do you dial for the police?
zh-film-en.ns00-02: Right: one, one, zero. But when grown-ups read out a number, they often don't say it that way. They say "yāo yāo líng." And the ambulance? "Yāo èr líng."
zh-film-en.ns00-03: In the army and on aircraft radios it gets even stranger: seven is "guǎi," and zero is "dòng."
zh-film-en.ns00-04: Why not just say "yī"? How did "qī" become "guǎi"? The answer is one word: noise.
zh-film-en.ns01-01: Noise is anything that damages your words on their way. A loud classroom, a crackly phone line... what you said arrives with a little bit missing.
zh-film-en.ns01-02: Let's try it. I'll say a number over the walkie-talkie. Listen: which number is it?
zh-film-en.ns01-03: Is it "yī" (one) or "qī" (seven)? Hmm... hard to tell, isn't it?
zh-film-en.ns01-04: Say them slowly: yī, qī. The second halves are exactly the same; the only difference is the tiny sound at the start. When noise covers it, qī sounds like yī.
zh-film-en.ns01-05: If you're giving an address and Building 7 is heard as Building 1, people go to the wrong place.
zh-film-en.ns01-06: Listen again. This time, a different word.
zh-film-en.ns01-07: Guǎi! You hear it at once. "Yāo" and "guǎi" sound nothing alike: even with a piece covered, one can't turn into the other.
zh-film-en.ns01-08: These names aren't random: the single dot on a die is called "yāo"; a 7 looks like a walking cane (guǎizhàng), so it's "guǎi"; a 0 looks like a hole, so it's "dòng."
zh-film-en.ns01-09: That's the first trick against noise: if two things sound alike, say them differently.
zh-film-en.ns02-01: Drawing has noise too. We played two rounds of Pictionary: the person drawing can't talk or write, only draw.
zh-film-en.ns02-02: Round one: free draw. Draw anything, and the guessers can guess anything.
zh-film-en.ns02-03: For this one, everyone guessed in turn: Egg? Alien? Baby?... After many guesses, someone finally shouted: It's Lucas!
zh-film-en.ns02-04: The drawing wasn't bad. A round face and two eyes: everyone has those, so it looks like anything.
zh-film-en.ns02-05: Same with the next one: "A triangle?" "A sheep?" "A dog?" Yes, a dog: our friend's corgi, Cashew!
zh-film-en.ns02-06: Round two uses twin cards. Each card has a pair of look-alikes, like umbrella and mushroom. Everyone can see both words; the person drawing flips a coin in secret to pick one.
zh-film-en.ns02-07: This round you only get 15 seconds to draw, and when time is up, the guessers get just one guess.
zh-film-en.ns02-08: Just a curved crescent? Some say banana, some say moon: fifty-fifty, just like a coin.
zh-film-en.ns02-09: But the drawers learned fast: give the umbrella a thin handle and it's guessed at once; add a few tiny stars and streaks of light around the star, and everyone changes their mind: "Oh, it's a star in the sky!"
zh-film-en.ns02-10: Those extra strokes are redundancy. Not just more drawing, but exactly the part that tells it apart from the others. Same idea as "yāo" and "guǎi."
zh-film-en.ns03-01: Last time we said redundancy is like a backup that helps a message survive noise. Today we saw one way it does that: make the things that are easy to mix up different.
zh-film-en.ns03-02: Claude Shannon also proved something amazing: if the extra bits are added cleverly enough, a message can get through noise almost word for word.
zh-film-en.ns03-03: But sometimes noise is sneakier: it quietly changes a word and doesn't let you notice. What then? Next time.
zh-film-en.ns03-04: Life has noise too: a loud classroom, being in a hurry, being upset. Is there something you'd really hate to be misheard? How would you say it so it reaches the other person safely? That's a question we learn and think about together at Lucas Academy.

en-film-zh.ns00-01: 考你一个问题：飞行员在无线电里要说字母 B，他们会怎么说？
en-film-zh.ns00-02: 不说「bee」。他们说「Bravo」。D 说「Delta」，T 说「Tango」。
en-film-zh.ns00-04: 为什么不直接说字母？为什么要给九多加一个音？答案就一个词：噪声。
en-film-zh.ns01-01: 噪声，就是在路上把消息弄坏的东西。吵闹的教室、沙沙响的电话……你说的话到了对方那里，就少了一点点。
en-film-zh.ns01-02: 来试一试。我在沙沙响的对讲机里说一个字母。你听：是哪个字母？
en-film-zh.ns01-03: B？D？还是 E？嗯……不太好说吧？
en-film-zh.ns01-04: 慢慢念：B、D、E、P、T、V。它们都以同一个长长的「ee」结尾，差别只在开头那一点点声音。噪声把那一点点盖掉，B 就变成了 D。
en-film-zh.ns01-05: 想象一下：飞行员把 B 听成了 D，把飞机开上了机场里错误的那条路。
en-film-zh.ns01-06: 再听一次。同样的沙沙声，换一个词。
en-film-zh.ns01-07: Bravo！一下就听出来了。Bravo 和 Delta 一点都不像，就算噪声吃掉一块，剩下的也足够分辨。
en-film-zh.ns01-08: 「niner」也是一样：多出来的那个音，让九在沙沙响的无线电里更容易听出来。
en-film-zh.ns01-09: 这就是对付噪声的第一招：两样东西听起来像，就把它们说得不一样。
en-film-zh.ns02-01: 画画也有噪声。我们玩了两轮你画我猜：画的人不能说话，也不能写字，只能画。
en-film-zh.ns02-02: 第一轮，自由画：想画什么都行，猜的人想喊什么都行。
en-film-zh.ns02-03: 这一张，大家猜了一个又一个：「鸡蛋？」「外星人？」「小宝宝？」……最后终于喊出：「Lucas！」
en-film-zh.ns02-04: 不是画得不好。一张圆脸、两只眼睛，几乎可以是任何人，所以看起来什么都像。
en-film-zh.ns02-05: 下一张也一样：「三角形？」「羊？」「一只狗？」对，是一只狗：朋友家的柯基，Cashew！
en-film-zh.ns02-06: 第二轮：双胞胎词卡。每张卡上是两样长得很像的东西，比如雨伞和蘑菇。两个词大家都看得见；画的人偷偷抛硬币，决定画哪一个。
en-film-zh.ns02-07: 这一轮只有十五秒，时间到了，猜的人只能猜一次。
en-film-zh.ns02-08: 只画一个弯弯的月牙？那就有人说香蕉，有人说月亮：一半一半，就跟抛硬币一样。
en-film-zh.ns02-09: 可是画的人很快学会了：给雨伞画上细细的伞柄，一猜就中；在星星周围添几颗小星星和几道光，大家马上改口：「哦，是天上的星星！」
en-film-zh.ns02-10: 多出来的这几笔就是冗余。不是随便多画，而是专门画那个能把它和别的分开的地方。和 Bravo 是同一个道理。
en-film-zh.ns03-01: 上一集我们说，冗余就像备份，帮消息扛过噪声。今天我们看到了它的一种用法：把容易混的东西变得不一样。
en-film-zh.ns03-02: 克劳德·香农还证明了一件神奇的事：只要多加的那些比特加得够聪明，消息就能穿过噪声，几乎不出错。
en-film-zh.ns03-03: 可噪声有时候更狡猾：它悄悄改掉一个字母，还不让你发现。那怎么办？下次再说。
en-film-zh.ns03-04: 生活里也有噪声：吵闹的教室、着急的时候、生气的时候。你有没有一句话，特别怕别人听错？你会怎么说，让它好好地传过去？这是我们在 Lucas Academy 一起学习、一起思考的问题。
